notes.meaning: Balaam set out early and eagerly. God had said he could go if the men came to call him, but he did not wait to be called. He got everything ready himself and rode off with Moab's leaders. The New Testament says Balaam rushed after money (Jude 11), and this eager start shows it.

God had allowed the trip, so why was He angry? Allowing something is not the same as approving it. Balaam went for the reward, and he secretly hoped to go against God's clear word. So the angel of the LORD stood in the road as an enemy to block him. The angel seemed like an enemy, but anyone who stops us on a sinful path is really our friend. Moab's leaders had likely gone on ahead, leaving Balaam with only his two servants.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critics think verse 22 clashes with God's permission in verse 20. They suggest the donkey story was added to the account later. Others answer that God was angry at Balaam's greedy heart on the way, not at the trip itself.

notes.meaning: The donkey saw the angel and his drawn sword, which was a sign of God's anger. Balaam, a man who boasted of seeing visions, saw nothing, because greed had blinded him. Instead of asking whether he was on the wrong road, he beat the donkey back onto it.

The angel then stood where a narrow path ran between vineyards, with low stone walls on both sides. The frightened donkey pressed against a wall and crushed Balaam's foot, so he beat her again. When trouble comes on our way, it is a good time to ask whether our path is right with God.

Last of all the angel stood where there was no room to turn at all, so the donkey lay down. Balaam flew into a rage and beat her with his stick. The three stops show how God often deals with stubborn sinners. First He gives a warning, then a light correction, and then a tight spot with no way out. People set on doing wrong often push right through the roadblocks God puts in their way.

This was a real miracle, a wonder done by God's power. The God who first gave people the power to speak could easily make a donkey speak, and 2 Peter 2:16 treats it as a real event. God used a lowly animal to teach a proud prophet a humbling lesson. The donkey's question was fair. When we want to strike someone with our hand or our words, we should first ask what they have really done to us.

differ.view: Some who fully accept the miracle say we cannot know exactly how it happened. God may have given the donkey human words, or He may have turned her cries into words that only Balaam understood.

notes.meaning: Strangely, Balaam argued with the donkey as if nothing odd had happened. His anger and greed had so blinded him that he did not stop to think. He wished he had a sword to kill her, yet he could not even kill his own donkey, let alone curse Israel. The donkey reminded him that she had served him faithfully for years and had never done this before. That alone should have told him something was wrong. We are given charge over animals, so we must not be cruel to them.
Only when God opened his eyes could Balaam see the angel. We can see neither God's anger nor His love unless He opens our eyes. Balaam fell facedown in awe and in fear of the sword.

The angel first scolded Balaam for beating his donkey, since God holds us to account for how we treat His creatures. Then came the real problem. Balaam's way was 'perverse', or crooked, because it grew from greed and was leading him to ruin. The donkey had actually saved his life. Without her, the angel would have killed Balaam and spared her. Often the very things that block us turn out to be God's kindness.

Balaam said, "I have sinned," but he quickly made an excuse: he had not seen the angel. He offered to go home only 'if' God was displeased, though he already knew God's mind. His fear was mostly fear of punishment, not a changed heart. As one writer puts it, many people leave their sins only because their sins have left them.

The angel let him go on, but repeated the warning: speak only what I tell you. The warning was repeated so Balaam could never claim he had not been told. It also told what would happen: instead of cursing Israel, he would be made to bless them. God allowed what He did not approve so that He could show His faithfulness to His people.

King Balak went all the way to his border on the Arnon River to greet Balaam. This was a great honor, and it was near where Israel was camped. But he quickly scolded Balaam for being slow and bragged that he could reward him richly. That showed pride, as if a prophet's message could be bought. We are slow to come to God, yet He is far more able to honor us than any king.

Balaam's reply sounds godly: he can only say what God puts in his mouth. It admits that a greater power was holding him back. Underneath, though, he seems annoyed at being held back and still eager to please Balak. He was trying to lower the king's hopes without telling him the whole truth.

They went on to Kiriath-huzoth, a name meaning 'city of streets'. Balak offered cattle and sheep as sacrifices and sent meat to Balaam and the leaders for a feast. The sacrifices were meant to win divine favor for the cursing ahead. The rich welcome was also meant to make Balaam feel he could refuse such a generous king nothing.

The next morning Balak took Balaam up to Bamoth-baal, which means 'high places of Baal', a hilltop where the idol Baal was worshiped. From there they could see the edge of Israel's camp. Balak thought Balaam needed to see the people for his curse to work. Balaam was now as eager to please Balak as he had once claimed to be to please God. It is a reminder to pray, "Lead us not into temptation."
